query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.material_initial_state: Selective-laser-melted Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy made from prealloyed powder. The as-printed material was a >97%-dense, single-fcc cellular microstructure with dislocation-rich cell walls; a comparison state was produced by direct aging and contained dual nanoprecipitates.
generation.intervention: The study compared the oxidation behavior of the as-printed alloy with material aged at 750°C for 50 h. Aging produced approximately 25–30 vol% homogeneously distributed Ni/Ti-enriched L12 nanoscale precipitates and larger Al/Ti-enriched, Cr/Fe-depleted L21 precipitates, mainly near cell walls. Both states were then subjected to isothermal oxidation.
generation.conditions: Polished 7.5 × 7.5 × 3 mm samples were oxidized for up to 96 h at 600, 750, 900, 1050, and 1200°C. Mass gain was monitored intermittently at 600–900°C, while oxide thickness was measured after 24, 48, 72, and 96 h at 900, 1050, and 1200°C. The reported atmosphere for oxidation was not explicitly specified.
generation.structural_mediator: Heating transformed the initial BCC/B2 substrate through FCC and Cr-Fe-rich sigma-phase formation at intermediate temperatures, followed by sigma dissolution at higher temperature. Oxidation generated an Al-rich external Al2O3 scale with a Cr-rich/Cr2O3 inner region; air produced a thick duplex scale and a pronounced Al-depleted, FCC/B2-denuded subsurface zone, whereas vacuum produced a much thinner scale and thin transformed subsurface layer.
generation.mechanism: Selective oxidation occurred primarily by outward diffusion of Al, and secondarily Cr, to react with oxygen. High oxygen availability accelerated scale growth and Al consumption, producing external Al2O3 over an inner Cr2O3-rich layer and driving Al depletion and phase transformation beneath the scale. Under low p(O2), slower oxidation kinetics limited scale growth. The alloy was assigned to the Group-III Giggins–Pettit regime because its high Al content supports a continuous external alumina scale.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-printed baseline, precipitation-aged material was expected to show higher oxidation mass gain, particularly as temperature increased, because Cr-depleted precipitates and precipitate–matrix boundaries impair or delay formation of the protective Cr-oxide layer. Nevertheless, both states were expected to retain broadly similar high-temperature oxide-growth activation energies and Cr2O3-mediated protection, so aging would provide strengthening without a large overall oxidation penalty.
generation.baseline: The baseline was the SLM as-printed, single-fcc cellular alloy with comparatively uniform Cr distribution and no L12/L21 nanoprecipitates; this uniform Cr distribution enabled earlier and easier formation of a protective Cr-rich oxide layer.
generation.boundary: The Cr-rich scale provided effective protection at lower temperatures, generally up to about 900°C. Mass-gain kinetics were mainly subparabolic at 750–900°C, although behavior at 600°C was near parabolic and the aged alloy returned to near-parabolic behavior at 900°C. Above 900°C, oxide-thickness growth was nearly parabolic, and increasingly rapid oxygen transport produced a substantial inner inhomogeneous oxide layer. Results cover isothermal exposures of no more than 96 h and 600–1200°C.

falsification_experiment.design: Time-resolved oxidation mass gain and power-law exponent/rate-constant fitting distinguished the two alloy states; cross-sectional SEM measurements quantified oxide-thickness growth and Arrhenius activation energies. SEM-EDS mapping identified elemental redistribution across the scale, while XRD and Raman spectroscopy identified Cr, Ti, elemental, and mixed/spinel oxides. Neutron diffraction and SEM characterized the initial fcc matrix and aged L12/L21 precipitates.
